source.text: וְ/אַתָּ֤ה שְׁכַב֙ עַל צִדְּ/ךָ֣ הַ/שְּׂמָאלִ֔י וְ/שַׂמְתָּ֛ אֶת עֲוֺ֥ן בֵּֽית יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עָלָ֑י/ו מִסְפַּ֤ר הַ/יָּמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תִּשְׁכַּ֣ב עָלָ֔י/ו תִּשָּׂ֖א אֶת עֲוֺנָֽ/ם־־־־׃

translation.text: And you, lie on your left side, and place the iniquity[a] of the house of Israel upon it; for the number of the days[b] that you lie on it, you shall bear their iniquity.

footnotes.text: Or 'guilt' or 'punishment for iniquity' for 'iniquity' (Hebrew עָוֹן) in both occurrences; the term can include the sin itself, its guilt, or its consequence.

Swete's Greek text (based here on Codex Vaticanus) specifies 'one hundred and fifty' days here, where the Hebrew gives no numeral. See the numerical differences noted at verses 5 and 9; the relationship between these readings remains unresolved.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Imperative of שׁכב in a physical posture command. 'Lie' is natural English and sufficiently direct; 'lie down' is possible but slightly more expansive than the Hebrew.
צַד commonly means 'side.' 'Your left side' is the most idiomatic and precise rendering for the commanded posture.
שׂים has a broad semantic range including 'put/set/place.' 'Place' fits the symbolic-action context and avoids overly colloquial wording.

עָוֹן can denote iniquity, guilt, or the burden/consequence of sin. In this enacted sign, Ezekiel symbolically carries Israel's sinful burden. 'Iniquity' preserves the moral dimension while allowing the bearing imagery to stand. The broader semantic possibility is preserved in a footnote.
The construct phrase is a standard collective designation. 'The house of Israel' preserves the covenantal-corporate wording of the Hebrew.
The pronoun most naturally refers back to 'side' in the symbolic action. 'Upon it' keeps the slightly formal, spatial sense and clarifies the object borne on the side.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the number of the days that
alternatives: according to the number of the days that
lexical_decisions.rationale: This phrase marks duration measured by a counted number of days. 'For the number of the days that' is readable while preserving the quantitative force of מִסְפַּר.
נשא with עָוֹן commonly means 'bear' iniquity/guilt. 'Bear' is the established and semantically apt English equivalent in moral-burden contexts.
The suffix is plural ('their'), referring to the house of Israel corporately. 'Their iniquity' matches the earlier עָוֹן and preserves lexical consistency within the verse.

theological_decisions.issue: Meaning of Ezekiel's symbolic bearing of Israel's עָוֹן
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain 'bear their iniquity' as a symbolic prophetic sign-act without importing substitutionary atonement language.
theological_decisions.rationale: The verse describes Ezekiel's enacted prophetic representation of Israel's burden. The Hebrew permits a range around sin/guilt/punishment, but the text itself does not require a developed atonement reading. Preserving 'bear their iniquity' maintains the theological tension and leaves interpretation open within the verse's symbolic context.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3 (Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it)

source.text: וַ/אֲנִ֗י נָתַ֤תִּֽי לְ/ךָ֙ אֶת שְׁנֵ֣י עֲוֺנָ֔/ם לְ/מִסְפַּ֣ר יָמִ֔ים שְׁלֹשׁ מֵא֥וֹת וְ/תִשְׁעִ֖ים י֑וֹם וְ/נָשָׂ֖אתָ עֲוֺ֥ן בֵּֽית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל־־־׃

translation.text: And I have assigned to you the years of their iniquity[a] according to the number of days, three hundred and ninety days[b], and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.

footnotes.text: Or 'the punishment of their iniquity' or 'their guilt'; the Hebrew word can refer to iniquity, guilt, or the punishment resulting from guilt.
Swete's Greek text (based here on Codex Vaticanus) reads 'one hundred and ninety days,' also in verse 9. The Hebrew has 390 in both verses; which number came first remains uncertain.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the verb is literally 'I have given,' in this context of imposing a symbolic period on Ezekiel, 'have assigned' communicates the sense of appointing or allotting a burdened duration without paraphrasing beyond the Hebrew.

The construct phrase literally reads 'the years of their iniquity.' In context, the following phrase 'according to the number of days' shows that years are being represented by days. Rendering עָוֹן as 'iniquity' preserves the moral sense of guilt rather than collapsing it into mere penalty, though the term can include the consequence of guilt.

עָוֹן can denote iniquity, guilt, or punishment borne for guilt. 'Iniquity' is retained in both occurrences to preserve lexical consistency and the theological weight of Israel's sin, while the bearing language allows the consequence-bearing nuance to remain implicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the number of days
alternatives: equal to the number of days
lexical_decisions.rationale: This phrase explains the symbolic correspondence between years and days. 'According to the number of days' is a natural English rendering that preserves the formal relationship indicated by לְ plus מִסְפָּר.
Straightforward cardinal number plus noun; rendered idiomatically in standard English number form.
נשא with עָוֹן commonly means 'bear' iniquity/guilt. 'Bear' preserves the established biblical idiom and the symbolic-prophetic force of Ezekiel's enacted sign.
The construct expression is a standard covenantal-national designation. 'The house of Israel' preserves the Hebrew form and its corporate sense better than the simpler 'Israel'.

theological_decisions.issue: Meaning of עָוֹן in a prophetic sign-act
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Rendered as 'iniquity' in both occurrences, while allowing the context of bearing to imply guilt and its burdened consequence.
theological_decisions.rationale: The verse concerns Ezekiel symbolically bearing Israel's sin over a set period. Translating עָוֹן as 'iniquity' avoids over-resolving whether the emphasis is on the sin itself, the guilt incurred, or the punishment borne; the Hebrew can encompass these related senses.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3, Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.

source.text: וְ/כִלִּיתָ֣ אֶת אֵ֗לֶּה וְ/שָׁ֨כַבְתָּ֜ עַל צִדְּ/ךָ֤ ה/ימיני שֵׁנִ֔ית וְ/נָשָׂ֖אתָ אֶת עֲוֺ֣ן בֵּית יְהוּדָ֑ה אַרְבָּעִ֣ים י֔וֹם י֧וֹם לַ/שָּׁנָ֛ה י֥וֹם לַ/שָּׁנָ֖ה נְתַתִּ֥י/ו לָֽ/ךְ־־־־׃

translation.text: When you have finished these, you shall lie down a second time on your right side, and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days. I have assigned you a day for each year[a].

footnotes.text: Hebrew: 'a day for a year, a day for a year.' The repeated wording emphasizes the symbolic correspondence between the days Ezekiel lies down and the years represented.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect with prefixed conjunction is rendered temporally in context, introducing the next symbolic action after the prior period is completed. 'These' refers to the preceding enacted signs/days.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall lie down a second time on your right side
alternatives: you shall lie on your right side again
you shall lie down on your right side a second time
lexical_decisions.rationale: שֵׁנִית modifies the repeated action, so 'a second time' is explicit. 'Lie down' is natural English for the enacted posture.

alternatives: you shall carry the punishment for
you shall bear the guilt of
lexical_decisions.rationale: נשא עון can denote bearing guilt/iniquity or its consequence. Here the prophet symbolically carries Judah's iniquity in an enacted sign. 'Bear the iniquity' preserves the Hebrew's theological breadth without over-resolving to either guilt or punishment alone.
The construct phrase is retained formally as 'house of Judah,' a standard prophetic designation for the southern kingdom/people.
English idiom naturally supplies 'for' with a duration of time.

alternatives: a day for a year, a day for a year
day for year, day for year
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated formula emphasizes proportional correspondence. In English, 'a day for each year' communicates the sense clearly while avoiding awkward literal repetition in the main text.

alternatives: I have given it to you
I have appointed it for you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The suffix likely refers to the day-year measure/period imposed on Ezekiel. 'Assigned' fits the context of divinely appointed symbolic duration better than the more generic 'given.'

theological_decisions.issue: Meaning of עָוֺן in the symbolic action
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain 'iniquity' rather than specifying only guilt or punishment
theological_decisions.rationale: In prophetic sign-acts, עָוֺן can encompass both the people's wrongdoing and the burden/consequence associated with it. Preserving 'iniquity' maintains the theological tension rather than narrowing the sense beyond what the Hebrew requires.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3: Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.

revisions.to: When you have finished these, you shall lie down a second time on your right side, and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah forty days; a day for a year, a day for a year, I have assigned it to you.
revisions.rationale: Retained the main wording but made the repeated Hebrew phrase explicit rather than compressing it to 'for each year.' Also rendered the final clause more literally as 'I have assigned it to you' and removed 'for' before 'forty days' for a slightly closer formal correspondence.

source.text: וְ/אֶל מְצ֤וֹר יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ תָּכִ֣ין פָּנֶ֔י/ךָ וּֽ/זְרֹעֲ/ךָ֖ חֲשׂוּפָ֑ה וְ/נִבֵּאתָ֖ עָלֶֽי/הָ־׃

translation.text: And toward the siege of Jerusalem you shall set your face, with your arm bared, and you shall prophesy against it[a].

footnotes.text: Or 'concerning it.' The Hebrew preposition can be broader, but here the context of siege and judgment supports 'against it.'

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a siege or state of besiegement. In this enacted-sign context, 'toward the siege of Jerusalem' is the most natural English rendering. 'Siegeworks' is possible in some contexts but is too concrete here without explicit reference to ramps or fortifications.
The Hiphil of כון with 'face' conveys directing or setting oneself resolutely toward something. 'Set your face' preserves the idiomatic force and prophetic solemnity better than a flatter paraphrase.
The phrase is verbless, literally 'and your arm exposed/uncovered.' 'With your arm bared' gives natural English while preserving the image of readiness for action or judgment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and you shall prophesy against it
alternatives: and you shall prophesy concerning it
and you shall speak prophetically against it
lexical_decisions.rationale: With נבא plus עַל, the sense commonly carries an adversative force in judgment contexts. Since the sign-act concerns Jerusalem under judgment, 'against it' best reflects the contextual force. The pronoun refers back to Jerusalem, rendered as 'it' in English for natural style.

theological_decisions.issue: Force of prophetic speech toward Jerusalem
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The prophecy is rendered as directed 'against' Jerusalem in keeping with the judgment context.
alternative_readings: The phrase could be rendered more neutrally as 'concerning it.'
theological_decisions.rationale: The preposition עַל can be broader than adversative English 'against,' but in Ezekiel's sign-act announcing siege and judgment, the hostile/judicial nuance is contextually primary. This preserves the text's severity without adding doctrinal interpretation beyond the immediate context.

translation.text: And behold, I have put ropes[a] on you, and you will not turn yourself from your side to your other side[b] until you have completed the days of your siege.

footnotes.text: Literally 'from your side to your side.'

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the attention-getting deictic force of the Hebrew while preserving prophetic solemnity. 'Behold' is slightly formal but still readable and matches the marked discourse function.
The perfect verb presents YHWH's action as effected. 'Put' is natural English with עַל in this context and avoids over-formality.
Direct and idiomatic with the verb 'put'; 'upon' would be more formal without adding meaning.
The noun denotes binding implements. 'Ropes' is the clearest modern English rendering; 'cords' is possible but less vivid, and 'bands' could sound metaphorical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you cannot turn yourself
alternatives: and you will not be able to turn yourself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Niphal here conveys being turned/turning oneself over from side to side in context. Rendering with inability ('cannot') best reflects the effect of the ropes in natural English, while 'turn yourself' preserves the bodily action.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from one side to the other
alternatives: from your side to your side
from one of your sides to the other
lexical_decisions.rationale: This idiomatic English captures the Hebrew expression of changing bodily position from side to side. A more literal rendering would sound awkward in English.

alternatives: until the completion of your acting out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construct with suffix marks the endpoint of Ezekiel's assigned action. 'Have completed' preserves the sense of finishing an appointed period with slightly greater gravity than 'finish'.
A straightforward formal rendering of the construct chain; 'days of' preserves the temporal concreteness of the sign-act.
In context of Ezekiel's enacted sign against Jerusalem, this refers to the siege represented by the prophet's action. 'Your siege' is the most natural and sufficiently precise rendering.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The phrase refers to the symbolic siege Ezekiel is enacting, not a literal siege against Ezekiel personally.
alternative_readings: A more wooden reading could leave the referent unexplained as 'your siege' without contextual clarification.
theological_decisions.rationale: The suffix is retained in translation, but the wording must still make sense in English. The context of Ezekiel 4 is a prophetic sign-act in which the prophet bears and depicts Jerusalem's siege. Rendering 'your siege' preserves the Hebrew form while allowing the contextual referent to remain implicit rather than over-explained.

revisions.rationale: Replaced 'so that you cannot' with the more direct 'and you will not' to reflect the Hebrew wording more closely; adjusted 'from one side to the other' to 'from your side to your other side' for closer correspondence to the source.

source.text: וְ/אַתָּ֣ה קַח לְ/ךָ֡ חִטִּ֡ין וּ֠/שְׂעֹרִים וּ/פ֨וֹל וַ/עֲדָשִׁ֜ים וְ/דֹ֣חַן וְ/כֻסְּמִ֗ים וְ/נָתַתָּ֤ה אוֹתָ/ם֙ בִּ/כְלִ֣י אֶחָ֔ד וְ/עָשִׂ֧יתָ אוֹתָ֛/ם לְ/ךָ֖ לְ/לָ֑חֶם מִסְפַּ֨ר הַ/יָּמִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר אַתָּ֣ה שׁוֹכֵ֣ב עַֽל צִדְּ/ךָ֗ שְׁלֹשׁ מֵא֧וֹת וְ/תִשְׁעִ֛ים י֖וֹם תֹּאכֲלֶֽ/נּוּ־־׀־־׃

translation.text: And you, take for yourself wheat and barley, beans and lentils, millet and spelt[a], and put them into one vessel, and make them into bread for yourself. For the number of the days that you lie on your side—three hundred and ninety days[b]—you shall eat it.

footnotes.text: Or 'emmer' or 'a kind of wheat' for 'spelt'; the exact identification of the ancient grain כֻסְּמִים is uncertain.
Swete's Greek text (based here on Codex Vaticanus) reads 'one hundred and ninety days,' also in verse 5. The Hebrew has 390 in both verses; which number came first remains uncertain.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperative plus dative pronoun is naturally reflexive/benefactive. 'Take for yourself' preserves the Hebrew force without sounding unnatural.
Standard rendering for the grain named here.
Standard rendering for the cereal grain.
A general English term is best in the main text; the more specific identification as broad/fava beans is plausible but too narrow for the main line without necessity.
Standard rendering.
The term is commonly identified as millet; this is the clearest modern equivalent.
Traditional and still plausible rendering for this grain term. Because exact ancient grain taxonomy is debated, alternatives are preserved in a footnote.
'Vessel' preserves the concrete sense of כְּלִי while remaining readable. 'One' is retained to reflect the Hebrew emphasis on combining them together.

lexical_decisions.chosen: make them into bread for yourself
alternatives: make bread from them for yourself
prepare them as bread for yourself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Hebrew literally has 'make them for yourself for bread.' 'Make them into bread for yourself' is idiomatic English that preserves both the transformation and the benefactive sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the number of the days
alternatives: according to the number of the days
lexical_decisions.rationale: This phrase introduces duration measured by the specified days. 'For the number of the days' keeps the formal structure while remaining understandable.

alternatives: you are lying on your side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle denotes the ongoing state in the enacted sign. English simple present works naturally in this instruction context.
The full written-out number suits Bible style and reflects the Hebrew wording.
The suffix is singular, referring back to the bread as a collective/singular item. 'You shall eat it' preserves the directive force.
